title: 'CRYPTID CONVERSATIONS' lectures on possible unexplained creatures
byline: Marley Roberson Senior Arts & Life Writer
excerpt: A prudish half-man, half-pig throws rocks at unsuspecting couples, an egregiously oversized possum skitters between drunken college parties and a hairy 8-foot-tall monster incites a manhunting mob.
content:
A prudish half-man, half-pig throws rocks at unsuspecting couples, an egregiously oversized possum skitters between drunken college parties and a hairy 8-foot-tall monster incites a manhunting mob.

Jess Tucker, an archivist at the university, and local author Jon Black presented “CRYPTID CONVERSATIONS” at the UNT CoLab, located at 207 N. Elm St. on Oct. 22. The married couple’s shared interest in the paranormal crafted a lively lecture discussing local lore and rumored cryptids.

“Both of us being from the area and we did have a lot of conversations about the paranormal lore and stuff that comes out of here,” Tucker said. “We were always fascinated by paranormal, supernatural stuff. There was a lot of early conversations about that. We’ve had a lot of adventures over the years, failed ghost hunts and things like that.”

The event was created in about three weeks, after CoLab director Kristen Kendrick asked Black if he would be interested in giving a talk. Black went to high school with Kendrick, and Tucker has collaborated with the CoLab on curating exhibitions through her work as an archivist for the past three years.

“It was just a very spontaneous opportunity where we already had set on the stage and they had the knowledge,” Kendrick said. “And so it was a really wonderful chance to just come together and have a fun evening and invite people who might be of the same mindset.”

Stepping inside the “belly of the beast,” the presenters of “CRYPTID CONVERSATIONS” dove into the nitty-gritty of human-animal hybrids, “hairy hominids” and lake monsters.

According to the presentation, there is not a universally agreed-upon definition of a cryptid. The term comes from “cryptozoology,” which is the search and study of animals not proven to exist. Some of the more recognized cryptids include Bigfoot, the Jackalope and the Loch Ness Monster. 

But to Black and Tucker, Denton may have cryptids of its own.

“I think a lot of times, folklore and cryptids give us a way to talk about things that are hard to talk about directly,” Tucker said. “Like, if you can tell the story about Oscar Washburn, then you can talk about racial violence in the context of a cryptid. Whereas, it’s a lot harder for most people to talk directly about Quakertown and about the very troubled racialized history we have.”

Old Alton Bridge, or “Goatman’s Bridge,” is rumored to be haunted by a half-man, half-goat figure that was murdered on the bridge in an act of racial violence. Though there are conflicting stories regarding the exact origin of the “Goatman,” the circumstances of the murder tell a greater story of Texas history.

Another mentioned cryptid was said to exist between the 1950s and 1980s, when stories circulated about a “Hogman” or “Pigman” who vandalised vehicles and terrified couples in an area near Bonnie Brae Street. Nicknamed “Hog Valley,” the area was a “lovers lane,” and the “Pigman” is said to have ventured out of the woods to throw rocks at unsuspecting couples. 

Again, there are conflicting origins of the “Pigman,” but there are theories the cryptid served the Cowboy Mafia, a ‘70s Texas drug smuggling ring, as a cautionary tale to keep people away from illegal operations.

“A lot of cryptid stories do have some very time-specific elements, like the Cowboy Mafia aspect of the pigman, parking on Lover’s Lane,” Black said. “That was a story that would only happen in certain decades.”

Some tales of local cryptids ended in town mobs being broken up by police after circulating rumors led to townwide manhunts for the creatures. Some more friendly cryptids, like a rumored 3-foot possum, not including the tail, have a nostalgic element. 

Black lived in Denton when rumors of the abnormally large possum circulated, and has a friend who claims to have seen it. 

“I’ve never seen anything,” Black said. “I’m much more into the folklore and cultural dynamics of cryptids than whether or not they actually exist.”

The possum with many names, “Old Pete,” “Battle Possum” and “MUS” (for marsupial of unusual size) is said to have lived in a student neighborhood between Welch Street and Carroll Boulevard in the 1990s.

“I feel like we, as the collective, we encounter these stories at certain times and places in our lives,” Black said. “And then you get that particular cryptid or legend, it becomes a really easy touchstone of going back to your feelings in that time and place.”
